choosing "ours" or "theirs", then run relevant verification.

## Pull Requests

Run `verify` before preparing a PR. A PR has a focused purpose without
accidental unrelated changes, and its description explains what changed, why,
how it was verified, and important compatibility or migration notes. Do not
claim checks were run if they were not.

## Destructive Operations

Treat `git reset --hard`, `git clean`, `git push --force`,
`git push --force-with-lease`, branch deletion, and rebase of shared history as
high-risk. Perform them only when explicitly requested or clearly required by an
approved workflow, and inspect what will be lost or rewritten before executing
them.

Check an external dependency only when its availability matters to the meaning
of readiness. Avoid readiness cascades (service A readiness → calls service B
readiness → calls service C …) without understanding the operational
consequences; prefer a lightweight check of the capability actually needed.

## Status Codes

Health endpoints return success when healthy and a non-success status when
unhealthy according to the configured probe policy; `HealthCheckOptions` allows
status-code mapping. Do not reuse business API status semantics mechanically for
orchestrator probes.

## Response Body

Keep probe responses small. When operators need detailed diagnostics, protect
that endpoint with network or authorization controls appropriate to the
environment.

## Exposure

Health endpoints often must be reachable by infrastructure without ordinary user
authentication. Choose exposure from the deployment topology: private/internal
network access, a dedicated management port, host restrictions, or authorization
where the probe infrastructure supports it.

## Startup Readiness

If initialization is asynchronous or slow, keep readiness unhealthy until the
required startup work has completed.

## Performance

Health checks may run frequently. Avoid expensive queries, long external
timeouts, large allocations, full business workflows, and Error-level logs for
every normal failed probe.

## Conditional and Cache Responses

### 304 Not Modified

Only for a conditional request (`If-None-Match`/ETag, `If-Modified-Since`)
when the client's cached representation is still valid. It carries no normal
representation and is not a generic "nothing changed" business response.

## Client Request Errors

### 400 Bad Request

The HTTP request itself is invalid: malformed JSON, invalid request shape,
model-binding failure, invalid formatting, missing required transport-level
input, or a request that cannot be interpreted according to the API contract.
With `[ApiController]`, many binding and validation failures are handled
automatically. Not for authentication failure.

### 406 Not Acceptable

The server cannot produce a representation acceptable under the client's
content negotiation. This concerns the response representation — do not confuse
it with `415`.

### 409 Conflict

Typical cases: a duplicate where uniqueness is part of the resource state; a
state transition incompatible with the current state; a conflicting concurrent
operation; an idempotency key reused with a different payload.

```text
Order already completed
    + request asks to cancel it
    -> 409 Conflict
```

Not for malformed request syntax.

### 412 Precondition Failed

The client supplied a conditional precondition that is false — for example
`If-Match: "version-7"` while the current version is `"version-8"`. That is
normally `412`, not a generic `409`, because an explicit HTTP precondition
failed.

### 415 Unsupported Media Type

The server does not support the request representation, for example
`Content-Type: application/xml` on a JSON-only endpoint. `415` concerns the
request body format; `406` concerns acceptable response formats.

### 422 Unprocessable Content

The request is syntactically and structurally valid, but its semantic or
business content cannot be processed — impossible business values, a business
rule rejection that is not a state conflict, a semantically invalid combination
of valid fields (for example `startDate > endDate`).

Some APIs deliberately use `400` for both transport and semantic validation;
follow an established project convention. For new APIs that distinguish them:

```text
400 -> invalid HTTP/request contract
422 -> structurally valid request, invalid semantics/business input
```

### 428 Precondition Required

The API contract requires a precondition the client did not provide, for example
a `PUT /api/orders/123` that requires `If-Match`:

```text
missing required If-Match -> 428
provided but stale If-Match -> 412
```

Use `428` for other mandatory preconditions only when the contract explicitly
defines them.

### 429 Too Many Requests

Rate limiting rejected the request. Include `Retry-After` when the server knows
when another attempt is appropriate. Do not represent validation failure as rate
limiting.

### 502 Bad Gateway

This API acts as an intermediary and received an invalid or unusable response
from an upstream service. Do not convert every dependency failure into `502`
mechanically.

### 503 Service Unavailable

The service is temporarily unable to handle the request: intentional
maintenance, a critical dependency unavailable for this operation, or temporary
overload when the service chooses `503` semantics. Include `Retry-After` when a
meaningful retry time is known.

### 504 Gateway Timeout

This API acts as an intermediary and an upstream service did not respond in
time. Do not return `504` for every internal `TaskCanceledException`;
distinguish a client-cancelled request, our own operation timing out, and an
upstream dependency timing out — the correct response depends on which occurred
and on the role this API plays.

## Idempotency

Method semantics matter for retries and duplicate handling: `GET` is safe and
idempotent; `PUT` is idempotent; `DELETE` is idempotent in intended state
semantics; `POST` is generally not idempotent.

For operations where a repeated `POST` must not create duplicate effects,
consider an idempotency key:

```http
Idempotency-Key: ...
```

The server associates the key with the request and result according to the API
contract; reuse of the same key with a materially different payload is a
reasonable `409`. Do not claim idempotency merely because duplicate requests
are unlikely.

## Optimistic Concurrency

When HTTP-level optimistic concurrency is part of the contract, prefer standard
conditional request semantics over custom status codes:

```text
GET           -> ETag: "v7"
PUT/PATCH     -> If-Match: "v7"
current is v7 -> update succeeds
current is v8 -> 412 Precondition Failed
If-Match required but absent -> 428 Precondition Required

Inspect `Process.Start`, shell execution, PowerShell/bash invocation, and
command arguments built from user input. Prefer APIs that separate executable
and arguments; validate or constrain external input when command execution is
genuinely needed.

## Path Traversal

Review user-controlled file names, paths, archive extraction, download paths,
and upload destinations for `../`, absolute-path injection, escaping the
intended root, and unsafe archive extraction. Normalize and verify that paths
remain within the intended storage boundary.

## SSRF

Inspect outbound requests where users can influence the scheme, host, port,
full URL, or redirect destination — especially when the server can reach
internal networks, metadata endpoints, or privileged services. Do not report
every user-supplied query parameter in an outbound request as SSRF;
host/control-plane influence matters.

## XSS / Unsafe HTML

For Angular, investigate deliberate sanitizer bypasses
(`bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, `bypassSecurityTrustScript`,
`bypassSecurityTrustResourceUrl`) and direct DOM manipulation with untrusted
content. Ordinary Angular binding benefits from framework escaping and
sanitization and is not automatically XSS. Review deliberate raw HTML handling in
any server-rendered UI as well.

## Unsafe Deserialization

Investigate dangerous polymorphic or type-driven deserialization, such as
`BinaryFormatter` or unsafe Newtonsoft `TypeNameHandling` configurations. Do not
deserialize untrusted payloads into arbitrary runtime types.

## Cryptography

Flag security-sensitive uses of MD5, SHA1, ECB mode, hardcoded encryption keys,
custom password hashing, and home-grown encryption protocols. Do not flag
MD5/SHA1 used solely as a non-security checksum. For passwords, established
password-hashing facilities such as ASP.NET Core Identity password hashers are
the expected mechanism, not reversible encryption.

  `docs/technology-stack.md`.

- Hooks are registered in exec form — `"command": "node"` with
  `"args": ["${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/<script>.mjs"]`, never a shell

  repository root they inspect from the hook input (`cwd`, or the edited file's
